idiom_name: Ordered[A] trait mixin (compare primitive), with Ordering[A] as the multi-ordering alternative
implementation_notes: Scala has no user-defined operator syntax, but symbolic method names like <, <=, >, >= are ordinary methods, so a trait can donate the whole relational family: extend Ordered[A], implement compare, and the concrete methods of the trait provide the operators (Ordered itself extends java.lang.Comparable). Ordered deliberately defines no equality - type erasure makes a sound default impossible - so equals/hashCode and CanEqual remain the developer's responsibility. Prefer scala.math.Ordering[A] when a type needs several orderings or when ordering should stay outside the class: instances are built with Ordering.by, Ordering.fromLessThan or Ordering.on, and Scala 3 can generate one with a derives clause. Keep the trait form for a single natural ordering of a value type.
pitfalls: Ordered does not define equals, and an Ordered instance whose compare returns 0 for unequal values is inconsistent by construction: override equals/hashCode to match compare, or use Ordering with an explicit equivalence.
Ordered is Java-Comparable-compatible, so it interacts with java.util collections' natural ordering - a mismatch between compare and equals propagates into TreeSet/TreeMap behaviour.

variants.name: Ordered[A] trait mixin (single natural ordering)
Ordering[A] type class (multiple orderings)
variants.implementation_notes: Keep ordering outside the type: create an Ordering[Version] (Ordering.by(v => (v.major, v.minor)), Ordering.fromLessThan, or Ordering.on), bring it into scope as an implicit (Scala 2) or given (Scala 3) value, and the same type can be ordered differently per call site - sorted, min, max and TreeSet all consume an implicit Ordering. Import scala.math.Ordering.Implicits._ to make the symbolic operators available on values whose Ordering is in scope. Choose this variant when several orderings coexist or when the type must not carry a natural ordering of its own.
variants.code_sketch:
object VersionOrderingExample {
  case class Version(major: Int, minor: Int)
  implicit val byVersion: Ordering[Version] = Ordering.by(v => (v.major, v.minor))

  val sorted = List(Version(1, 10), Version(1, 2)).sorted  // uses the implicit instance
  val values = List(Version(1, 10), Version(1, 2))
  val byMinor = values.min(Ordering.by[Version, Int](_.minor)) // a different ordering, per call site
}
pitfalls: An implicit or given Ordering must be in scope at the call site; a local instance that shadows a companion instance silently changes sorting order without touching the type.
Ordering and Ordered are only interchangeable through the implicit conversions in their companions (Ordering.Implicits._), so importing them changes which comparisons compile.

variants.name: Scala 3 derived Ordering (compiler-generated instance)
variants.implementation_notes: Scala 3 generates a given Ordering[P] = Ordering.derived for a type that declares derives Ordering, deriving memberwise ordering through a Mirror - the closest Scala gets to a compiler-generated operator family and the analogue of a defaulted C++20 comparison. The derived instance obeys the same limits as other derivations: order follows declaration order, only products/sums whose element types have Ordering instances qualify, and the failing field is reported at the derives clause.
variants.code_sketch:
case class Version(major: Int, minor: Int) derives Ordering

List(Version(1, 10), Version(1, 2)).sorted   // uses the derived instance
pitfalls: Derived ordering follows declaration order, so adding or reordering fields changes comparison semantics without any code change at the comparison site.
A field type without an Ordering instance makes derivation fail at the derives clause rather than at the offending field, which makes large models harder to diagnose.
